lessons.title: Preparing the work area and the working sample
lessons.html:
Preparing the work area and the working sample

A purity analysis tells the seed company and the farmer what is really in a seed lot. A bag sold as maize, wheat or lucerne seed should contain mostly pure seed of that kind. The analysis finds how much is other crop seed, weed seed and inert matter such as soil, stones and broken pieces.

Prepare the work area

  • Clean the purity bench completely before you start. Brush off all seeds and dust from the last sample so that they do not mix with the new one.
  • Check that the balance is level, clean and checked with test weights as your laboratory procedure says.
  • Have your tools ready: forceps, spatulas, sieves, a magnifier or lamp with magnifier, a blower if used, labelled trays or dishes.
  • Have reference material ready, such as a seed collection or identification book, so you can identify weed seeds.
  • Make sure lighting is good. Poor light causes mistakes.

Obtain the working sample

The sample sent to the laboratory is called the submitted sample. You do not analyse all of it. You reduce it to a smaller working sample using a divider, such as a riffle or centrifugal divider, or by the halving method. The aim is a working sample that represents the whole submitted sample.

  1. Mix the submitted sample well.
  2. Divide it again and again until you reach the working sample weight required by the testing rules your laboratory follows (usually ISTA rules) for that crop.
  3. Weigh the working sample and record the weight to the required number of decimal places.

Documentation

Check the sample number, crop, cultivar, lot number and the tests requested on the submission form. Write the sample number on every tray and on the worksheet. Never work on two samples on the bench at the same time. A mixed-up sample makes the whole result worthless.

lessons.title: Separating and identifying the components
lessons.html:
Separating and identifying the components

The working sample is separated by hand into components. The testing rules give definitions of what counts as pure seed for each crop. Learn these definitions well, because they decide where each particle goes.

ComponentWhat it includes
Pure seedSeeds of the species being tested, including pieces larger than the size set in the rules
Other seedsSeeds of other crops and weed seeds
Inert matterSoil, sand, stones, chaff, stems, small broken pieces, and other material that is not seed

How to separate

  1. Spread a small amount of the working sample on the bench.
  2. Use forceps or a spatula to move each particle into the correct tray: pure seed, other seeds, inert matter.
  3. Use the magnifier for small seeds and for doubtful particles.
  4. Work through the whole working sample in this way.

Identifying other seeds

Name each kind of other seed found. Some weed seeds may be prohibited or restricted in terms of seed legislation, and finding even one can affect whether the lot can be sold. Examples on South African farms include seeds of weeds such as thorn apple (stinkblaar) and others on the official list. If you cannot identify a seed, keep it aside and ask a senior analyst. Never guess.

Weighing the components

Weigh each component separately. Add the weights together and compare with the starting weight of the working sample. If there is a large loss or gain, beyond what your laboratory procedure allows, something has gone wrong, for example seeds were lost on the floor or the balance was not zeroed. The analysis must then be repeated.

Calculate each component as a percentage of the total weight of the components. Round results according to the rules. Record the names and number of other seeds found.

lessons.title: Retaining samples and completing the analysis
lessons.html:
Retaining samples and completing the analysis

After the analysis, the separated components and the rest of the submitted sample must be kept. If a customer or inspector questions the result, the laboratory must be able to check the work again.

Retain the components

  • Put each component in a labelled envelope or container with the sample number and component name.
  • Pure seed may be needed for other tests, such as germination, so pass it on as your procedure says.
  • Keep prohibited weed seeds found in the sample, because they are evidence.

Retain the submitted sample

Return the unused part of the submitted sample to its bag, seal it, label it and store it in the sample store. Storage should be cool and dry, safe from rodents and insects, so that the sample stays the same. Keep the sample for the period required by your laboratory procedure and seed legislation.

Complete the process

  1. Check your calculations. The percentages of pure seed, other seeds and inert matter should add to 100.
  2. Fill in the worksheet completely: sample number, working sample weight, component weights, percentages, names of other seeds, your name and the date.
  3. Hand the worksheet to the senior analyst for checking and signing.
  4. Clean the bench, tools and balance so that nothing is carried to the next sample.
  5. Record any problem, such as a sample that was damaged or a balance that failed its check.

Why accuracy matters

A farmer who plants a seed lot with weed seeds may spread a weed across a whole land. A seed company that sells seed below standard can lose its reputation and face legal action. Your careful work protects both.

Key points

  • Start with a clean bench and a checked balance, one sample at a time.
  • Reduce the submitted sample to a working sample with a divider so it stays representative.
  • Separate into pure seed, other seeds and inert matter using the rule definitions.
  • Never guess a weed seed; ask a senior analyst.
  • Label and keep components and the submitted sample in proper storage.

quiz.question: What are the three main components separated in a purity analysis?

options.text: Pure seed, other seeds and inert matter

quiz.question: Why is a divider used to make the working sample?

options.text: So the working sample represents the whole submitted sample

quiz.question: Which of these counts as inert matter?

options.text: Whole seeds of the crop being tested

quiz.question: What should you do with a seed you cannot identify?

options.text: Keep it aside and ask a senior analyst

quiz.question: The component weights add up to much less than the working sample weight. What does this mean?

options.text: Something went wrong and the analysis must be repeated
The balance must be thrown away

quiz.question: You can work on two samples on the bench at the same time to save time.
The unused part of the submitted sample must be sealed, labelled and stored.
Which steps are part of preparing the work area? (select all that apply)

options.text: Brushing all seeds and dust off the bench
Having reference material for weed identification
